source.text: הִנְ/נִ֥י עֹשֶׂ֛ה אֶת כָּל מְעַנַּ֖יִ/ךְ בָּ/עֵ֣ת הַ/הִ֑יא וְ/הוֹשַׁעְתִּ֣י אֶת הַ/צֹּלֵעָ֗ה וְ/הַ/נִּדָּחָה֙ אֲקַבֵּ֔ץ וְ/שַׂמְתִּי/ם֙ לִ/תְהִלָּ֣ה וּ/לְ/שֵׁ֔ם בְּ/כָל הָ/אָ֖רֶץ בָּשְׁתָּֽ/ם־־־־׃

translation.text: Behold, at that time I will deal with all your oppressors[a][f], and I will save the lame and gather the outcast[b], and I will make them praised and renowned[e] in every land[c] where they were put to shame[d].

footnotes.text: Or 'those who afflict you.' The Hebrew verb can denote afflicting, oppressing, or humbling.
Or 'the one who limps' and 'the one driven away'; the Hebrew uses feminine singular forms, likely personifying the afflicted community.
The Hebrew ends with ‘their shame.’ ‘Where they were put to shame’ is a contextual expansion, not a literal relative clause; the compressed phrase's grammatical attachment remains uncertain.
Literally ‘for praise and for a name.’ The main wording makes the public-honor sense explicit, replacing the Hebrew noun imagery with English predicates.

Selected Greek texts have action ‘in you, for your sake’ rather than explicitly against all oppressors, and a plural ‘they will be put to shame’ with no subject named in that clause. Rahlfs–Hanhart numbers the shame clause in 3:20; Swete prints it in 3:19. Align the content across these different divisions. Published Hebrew fragments partly support the received oppressors wording; they contain damaged or supplied letters. Neither exact lost Hebrew nor historical priority is established.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Introduces a solemn divine announcement. 'Behold' preserves the prophetic force better than the more colloquial 'look' or 'see'.

alternatives: I am about to act against
lexical_decisions.rationale: The received Qal participle עֹשֶׂה governs the explicit object all-your-afflicters. Retain ‘deal with’ provisionally without Latin's stronger killing claim. Published4Q77/Mur88 report object wording with letter uncertainty; selectedGreek in-you/for-you is different wording, not proof of exact lostHebrew. Future English remains the common restoration-context input, not newly certified; historical priority held. No fresh HALOT consultation.

Piel active participle plural with2fs suffix describes those afflicting/oppressing the feminine addressee. Published directHebrew copies partly support the object sequence, not an undamaged whole clause or received pointing. Retain ‘your oppressors’ provisionally; no physical-copy chronological winner or fresh ink reading. No fresh HALOT consultation.
A standard prophetic temporal formula. 'At that time' is the direct rendering of the Hebrew phrase here; 'on that day' would import a different common formula not used in this clause.
The verb ישׁע commonly denotes saving/delivering. 'Save' preserves the theological resonance while fitting the restoration context.
Literally 'the one who limps,' feminine singular used collectively or personifying the afflicted community. 'The lame' is idiomatic English and preserves the image.
From נדח, 'to drive away/scatter.' 'The outcast' communicates both exclusion and displacement in concise English.
A common restoration verb for assembling the scattered people. 'Gather' is direct and preserves biblical intertextual resonance.
The idiom with following predicates ('for praise and for a name') is best rendered 'make them,' expressing transformed status.

BDB explicitly cites3:19,20 for figurative praise/object-of-praise public status. English predicate ‘praised’ communicates that status with less opaque noun syntax but more readily suggests actual acclaim; this is a real semantic narrowing/loss of noun imagery, judged warranted moderately in context. No speaker, ceremony or motive added. Hebrew remains a noun; not a new morphological analysis. Pair reversal with20 preserved. No fresh HALOT consultation.

BDB explicitly associates the name idiom in3:19,20 with reputation/fame/glory. ‘Renowned’ makes that contextual sense explicit while sacrificing literal name-as-noun imagery. The one masked comparison favors this paired rendering moderately, not uniquely. Order praise/name in19 versus name/praise in20 remains praised/renowned versus renowned/praised. No new Hebrew wording or fresh HALOT consultation.
Although הארץ can mean 'earth,' in this restoration context with dispersion/shame among the nations, 'every land' better conveys the distributive sense of places where they had been scattered.

lexical_decisions.chosen: where they were put to shame
lexical_decisions.rationale: The pointed word is a shame noun with3mp suffix, not separately a preposition, relative marker or finite passive. ‘Where they were put to shame’ remains a provisional contextual expansion, not newly certified by the honor trial. Mur88's published noun is unbracketed/unmarked;4Q77's corresponding tail is supplied. Greek instead has a plural future passive without a named subject in that clause; RH numbers it3:20 whereas Swete prints it3:19. Align content rather than infer absence from numbering. Latin has a shame nounphrase. Do not claim uniform versional support or literal in-their-shame. No fresh HALOT consultation.

theological_decisions.issue: Restoration language for the afflicted remnant
alternative_readings: the limping one ... the driven-away one
theological_decisions.rationale: The feminine singular participles likely personify daughter Zion or function collectively for the afflicted people. The chosen English keeps the communal restoration sense without erasing the concrete imagery of weakness and exile.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.

source.text: בָּ/עֵ֤ת הַ/הִיא֙ אָבִ֣יא אֶתְ/כֶ֔ם וּ/בָ/עֵ֖ת קַבְּצִ֣/י אֶתְ/כֶ֑ם כִּֽי אֶתֵּ֨ן אֶתְ/כֶ֜ם לְ/שֵׁ֣ם וְ/לִ/תְהִלָּ֗ה בְּ/כֹל֙ עַמֵּ֣י הָ/אָ֔רֶץ בְּ/שׁוּבִ֧/י אֶת שְׁבוּתֵי/כֶ֛ם לְ/עֵינֵי/כֶ֖ם אָמַ֥ר יְהוָֽה־־׃

translation.text: At that time I will bring you in, and at that time I will gather you; for I will make you renowned and praised[b] among all the peoples of the earth, when I restore your fortunes[a] before your eyes, says Yahweh.

footnotes.text: Or, more literally, 'when I restore your captivity' or 'when I bring back your captives.' The Hebrew idiom refers broadly to restoring those who have suffered exile or calamity.
Literally ‘for a name and for praise.’ ‘Renowned and praised’ expresses public honor while preserving the reversed order of the paired terms from the preceding verse.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Temporal phrase introducing the promised future act. 'At that time' is idiomatic modern English and preserves the prophetic timing formula.

Hiphil of בוא commonly means 'bring in/bring'. 'Bring you in' best reflects the causative nuance and likely sense of bringing the exiles into their restored place, without over-specifying 'back' where the object/location is implicit rather than explicit.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and at the time when I gather you
alternatives: and at the time of my gathering you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive construct with suffix expresses the time of God's gathering them. 'At the time when I gather you' keeps the parallelism with the previous clause while remaining natural English.
Here כִּי introduces the ground or explanation for the preceding promise. 'For' preserves the explanatory force cleanly.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I will make you renowned and praised
alternatives: I will set you for renown and praise
I will make you renowned and praised
lexical_decisions.lexicon: BDB printed240 sense5c and1028 name2b(1); WLC/OSHB
lexical_decisions.rationale: The paired noun idiom denotes public reputation and praise. English renowned/praised predicates make that status explicit and preserve the reversed order from19. This loses noun/name imagery and praised can suggest actual acclaim more strongly than object-of-praise; the one masked preference judges this tradeoff warranted moderately, not uniquely. Hebrew nouns/pointing remain exact. Shared gathering-time/fortunes wording not newly certified. No fresh HALOT consultation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: among all the peoples of the earth
alternatives: among all the peoples of the land
with all the peoples of the earth
lexical_decisions.rationale: 'Among' fits the social setting of reputation before the nations. הָאָרֶץ here is best taken globally ('earth') in this restoration oracle, not merely 'land.' 'Peoples' preserves the plural עמים.

alternatives: when I bring back your captives
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom שוב שבות regularly denotes restoration from calamity/exile. In contemporary English, 'restore your fortunes' communicates the idiomatic sense better than the wooden 'restore your captivity,' while not excluding return from exile.
A transparent idiom meaning the restoration will be openly witnessed by them. 'Before your eyes' is vivid and natural.

Align metadata with the existing actual English and declared doctrine: יְהוָה is rendered Yahweh, not the LORD. This repairs the contradictory old rationale without changing source or selecting a new divine-name rendering; the old entry is archived, not silently erased. No fresh HALOT consultation.

theological_decisions.rationale: The verse uses the Tetragrammaton יְהוָה directly. Per updated doctrine, the divine name is rendered 'Yahweh' rather than 'the LORD', preserving the covenant name God revealed at Sinai.

The Hebrew idiom can be rendered woodenly, but optimal equivalence favors the established idiomatic sense of comprehensive restoration. This avoids importing a narrower meaning while still fitting the exile-restoration context.
